data.title: Stork options: Singaporeâs IVF market sees patient demand amid birth dearth
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] More would-be parents are trying for babies with the help of modern medicine – and this is leaving the field wide open for operators in the fertility health segment. 

In a 2024 report, consulting firm Kearney identified Singapore as “a prime example of a mature in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) market”, with widespread access and partial public funding contributing to a high penetration rate of more than seven cycles per 1,000 women.

Organic demand aside, a revamp of the government’s marriage and parenthood measures could also boost the fertility market and provide uplift to private healthcare players.

Fertility and maternal health are already issues under review by Singapore’s national Marriage and Parenthood Reset Workgroup, Minister in the Prime Minister’s Office Indranee Rajah announced in October. That is as the country’s total fertility rate (TFR) fell to a historic low of 0.87 in 2025, from 0.97 in 2024.

The workgroup, which she chairs, is expected to release a fresh slate of policy recommendations in early 2027. When that happens, watchers are not ruling out enhancements to government subsidies that could widen patients’ assisted reproductive technology (ART) options.

Booming demand

Though Singapore-specific data is hard to come by, the value of the Asia-Pacific ART market is estimated to be in the billions of dollars.

One cycle of IVF at a public clinic could set would-be parents back by S$15,000 to S$18,000, while private facilities charge around S$20,000 to S$25,000. The Ministry of Health (MOH) disclosed in 2024 that IVF cycle costs at public hospitals rose by about 2 per cent each year in the decade prior.

The number of ART treatment cycles carried out in Singapore nearly doubled in the last decade or so – from 5,800 in 2013 to 10,500 in 2022, according to figures previously reported by MOH.

Singapore’s more than a dozen licensed assisted reproduction centres comprise three public hospitals, as well as a number of private healthcare providers – which are seeing robust demand for fertility services, most notably IVF and related procedures.

At mainboard-listed Thomson Medical, more than 6,000 patients sought procedures such as IVF, intrauterine insemination (IUI), and egg and sperm freezing in the year to end-June – and “we have been able to maintain a relatively stable demand” for fertility services year on year, acting CEO Cassandra Loh tells The Business Times.

Meanwhile, Singapore Medical Group (SMG), a subsidiary of CHA Healthcare, ascribes about half of its overall business volume to women’s health, fertility and related services.

Chris Chung, CEO of CHA Asia Pacific, and Beng Teck Liang, CEO of SMG, jointly say: “Assisted fertility is becoming a key pillar of our women’s and reproductive health business.”

A spokesperson for IHH Healthcare, whose portfolio includes Mount Elizabeth Fertility Centre, added: “We remain positive about the outlook for the assisted fertility market in Singapore.”

He cites delayed parenthood as one factor that is expected to continue driving demand for fertility services, alongside greater consumer awareness and medical advancements.

When the idea was mooted in Parliament by then MP Louis Ng in 2020, MOH replied that public centres had enough capacity, though it did not rule out studying the proposal to extend co-funding to the private sector “while ensuring charges remain reasonable”.

But Minister for Health Ong Ye Kung told Parliament in February 2026 that various fertility health policies were being reviewed, including financial support for assisted conception procedures – a point that he reiterated at a subsequent parliamentary sitting in October.

“One of the key structural business challenges for private fertility providers in Singapore is competing for patients without access to the same financing support available in the public sector,” says Choy Shook Yee, chief commercial officer of Temasek-backed Foundation Healthcare, which listed on the Singapore Exchange’s mainboard in mid-2026. 

That lack of co-funding “creates a different cost proposition for private providers and can influence patient choice, particularly given the costs involved in fertility treatment”, she adds.

Upcoming policy changes could include increases in government co-funding for ART, higher MediSave claim limits and more funded ART cycles, suggests Institute of Policy Studies senior research fellow Tan Poh Lin, who researches women’s fertility in Asia. Such initiatives could “help to offset the financial expenses” faced by would-be parents, she notes.

Seminal support

The Singapore government offers co-funding of up to 75 per cent for assisted conception procedures – such as IVF, IUI, and the testing of embryos for genetic diseases before they are implanted in the womb.

In IVF, embryos are created by fertilising eggs with sperm in a laboratory. IUI involves inserting pre-selected sperm directly into the uterus during ovulation.

The co-funding is available only for services at public hospitals. Between 2023 and 2025, MOH provided more than S$20 million a year in co-funding, mainly for IVF, a spokesperson for the ministry tells BT. 

Patients can also use MediSave to pay for treatment at both public and private hospitals, up to a lifetime cap of S$15,000. MediSave claims for assisted conception in this three-year period also totalled more than S$20 million annually, according to the MOH spokesperson.

Most IVF cycles are performed in public assisted reproduction centres, says the spokesperson, and the market share has remained stable over the three years. “However, (the) private-sector’s share of MediSave (amounts) claimed is increasing, arising from higher withdrawals per claim, which could be due to the charges by private providers.”

Within the last five years, MOH has embarked on notable efforts to increase the collective ART capacity at the three public hospitals by about 20 per cent.

Yet, Chung and Dr Beng say that public-sector capacity may still be strained because “the current funding structure creates a strong financial incentive to choose public hospitals”. 

Private ART providers tell BT that extending subsidies to the private sector could broaden access for patients, which is significant because time is of the essence for conception.

In Australia, where CHA Asia Pacific and SMG are invested in IVF provider City Fertility, Chung and Dr Beng note the government offers partial rebates for IVF costs at some private centres.

“This (government) support has helped normalise fertility treatment as part of mainstream healthcare, improving access for patients who need it,” they remark.

But, even if funding is extended to private providers, companies do not expect an instant bonanza. “From a patient perspective, any subsidy should ideally translate into reduced out-of-pocket costs while maintaining transparency in billing,” the IHH spokesperson notes.

Any changes to funding “could also encourage providers to continually review their care delivery models to ensure that treatments remain accessible, sustainable and competitively priced”, he says, adding that IHH would also review its fee structure to take into account factors such as clinical requirements, quality standards and “prevailing market conditions”.

Thomson Medical’s Loh says the most immediate impact of expanded co-funding would be a smaller price gap between public and private options.

She tells BT: “There may be some adjustments to the fee structure in the private market, but as pricing has been quite stable across the board, we do not anticipate major shifts in the overall market.”

But co-funding may not result directly in higher procedure volumes, she cautions, since any boost to private-sector demand from potential funding enhancements would ultimately depend on factors such as eligibility criteria, funding limits and approved procedures.

“More fundamentally, we think any policy should balance patient access and clinical outcomes, alongside the prudent use of public funds,” she adds.

Costs and competition

Putting aside the potential for broader access to government funds, procedure prices in the private market are also contingent on business factors such as operating costs.

The IHH spokesperson notes that the assisted fertility industry “requires significant investment in clinical expertise, technology, laboratory capabilities and quality assurance”.

And, even as demand for ART services is booming, the Singapore market has only “a limited pool of highly specialised fertility specialists”, Foundation Healthcare’s Choy notes.

As a result, competition is based “not only on price, but also on clinical outcomes, patient experience, accessibility and continuity of care”, she says.

Another hurdle: Singapore medical providers risk losing revenue to cheaper peers overseas.

After all, the cost of IVF could be 74 per cent lower in Malaysia than in Singapore, Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute senior fellow Lee Poh Onn noted in an article in December 2025.

Said Dr Lee then: “The cost attractiveness of medical procedures in Malaysia (and Johor) is perhaps the most significant factor attracting medical tourists from neighbouring countries.”

While MOH does not track Singaporeans who opt for IVF abroad, obstetrician and gynaecologist Paul Tseng, the medical director of Foundation Healthcare subsidiary CareIVF, notes that Singapore sits in “an inherently competitive regional healthcare market”.

“We are mindful that some patients may opt to consider neighbouring countries where treatment can be offered at lower costs,” says Dr Tseng.

Some industry players hold up their regional partnerships as a selling point.

For instance, Thomson Medical already offers fertility services in both Singapore and Malaysia, with TMC Fertility branches in Johor Bahru, Kota Damansara and elsewhere.

Loh of Thomson Medical says: “For patients who are considering cross-border options, that gives us an opportunity to provide greater continuity across markets where appropriate, while working within the respective clinical and regulatory frameworks.”

For SMG, parent company CHA’s IVF portfolio in Australia, Japan and South Korea acts as another selling point that “differentiates our offering”, say Chung and Dr Beng.

“Patients can access specialist expertise, second opinions and cross-border treatment options while maintaining continuity of care at home within an integrated healthcare network,” they tell BT.

But, acknowledging that they cannot entirely compete on cost, Singapore healthcare operators instead emphasise the quality of the service that they are able to offer here.

Says Choy: “At CareIVF, our approach is to keep our services competitively priced while leveraging (Foundation Healthcare’s) broader specialist network, allowing patients to access consultations and follow-up care conveniently across Singapore.”

Meanwhile, the spokesperson for IHH, which is dual-listed in Singapore and Malaysia, notes that the company’s Gleneagles Hospital Johor does see Singapore-based patients – but typically for simpler procedures, such as health screenings, endoscopy or cataract surgery.

Though Singaporeans could undergo fertility treatments across the Causeway, “we don’t encourage it”, the spokesperson added.

Instead, he stressed the benefits of “a seamless treatment journey from consultation through to follow-up” and pointed to potential difficulties in the cross-border management of confidential or protected patient data.

“No choice”

Since 2023, an annual average of about 4,000 patients have benefited from government co-funding for assisted conception, while about 5,000 patients have made MediSave withdrawals for such procedures each year, the MOH spokesperson tells BT.

He adds that the ministry “will continue to engage Singaporeans on fertility health, and work closely with stakeholders and the community as we develop recommendations” on policy.

Singapore Management University sociologist Paulin Tay Straughan, who specialises in issues of family, work and ageing, thinks enhancements to government support for ART are both inevitable and “a practical response” to delayed marriage and childbearing.

“More and more (couples) need help, and help is expensive. So the inevitability comes now because we have no choice – we have to support those who need help,” she notes.

Still, Prof Straughan is worried that the government footing the bill for more reproductive health-related expenses “may send the wrong message that it is alright to wait” to have children, given that success rates for assisted fertility procedures decline with age.

Despite the lower success rate, Dr Tan of the Institute of Policy Studies thinks there will still be interest, because rising maternal ages will increase the size of this subgroup. She says older mothers are often also highly motivated to have another child.

Still, she warns: “Singapore’s low TFR ultimately arises from social root causes, and initiatives through public health or technological solutions can only do so much.”

data.title: Secretlab opens first experience store in Los Angeles, targets S$500 million in global revenue
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Secretlab is taking its products into US stores for the first time, as the Singapore-founded chair and desk maker sets its sights on S$500 million in global revenue.

The company – established in 2015 and best known for its gaming chairs – opened its first overseas experience store in Los Angeles on Friday (Nov 13). It is also setting up a collaboration with retail giant Best Buy to set up displays in 15 stores in nine states.

The S$500 million target is about 35 per cent higher than Secretlab’s FY2024 revenue of S$370.7 million for the year ended February 2024. It made S$34.7 million in profit that same year, according to data from the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority seen by The Business Times.

Its FY2025 and FY2026 accounts were not filed in the records.

Secretlab said that it has sold S$2.5 billion worth of products worldwide since it started 11 years ago, with North America contributing half of its global revenue. The company revealed that it has more than three million users around the world.

Singapore shows significance of physical retail

Even without a physical store there, the US is already Secretlab’s largest market, said Ian Ang, co-founder and CEO of Secretlab, in an exclusive interview with BT.

In comparison, Singapore – the only country in which Secretlab has a physical presence – accounts for less than 2 per cent of revenue.

For Secretlab, the US is around “30 times the size of Singapore”, he noted.

Yet, Singapore is where the brand reaches furthest.

Among all its markets, Singapore has the “highest saturation by far”, Ang pointed out, adding that the reach extends far beyond gamers, with some law firms and even clinics using Secretlab chairs in their offices.

This is less common overseas, he said.

He measures saturation in what he describes as a “very layman way”: Secretlab sales in a country against its gross domestic product, adjusted for income levels.

Ang posits the reason why Singapore has such a high saturation rate is because of its retail presence. Having a physical presence will allow potential buyers to try and experience the products, he felt. “You need to experience it in order to really appreciate how good the product is.”

Beyond its experience centre located in Braddell, Secretlab has also participated in four to six IT shows in Singapore annually over the past decade, noted Ang.

Not a stranger to the US

The US is a familiar market for Secretlab. The brand has established a following among gamers in the world’s largest economy by sponsoring top global gaming teams.

The company has also established a physical presence through pop-up booths at gaming tournaments and events.

Ang noted that Secretlab held back from opening a brick-and-mortar store in the US earlier because of the lack of variety in its product line. “The store might look bare,” he said.

Now, in addition to a wider range of designs among its chairs, Secretlab has also added tables and other desktop accessories to its product line. This could lift how much each customer spends, explained Ang.

Criteria for success

For the big overseas push to work, the sales in the US have to pass two tests, Ang pointed out.

First, it must pay for itself. “We are not a VC (venture capital)-backed company, so we need to make sure that whatever we do, the returns are definitely there,” he said. “A lot of retail initiatives lose money… You cannot just lose money. How much are you losing relative to how much you are potentially gaining?”

Asked how the expansion will be funded, Ang pointed to the company’s “financial discipline”, but he did not name a source of funds.

The second test is scale. This means that the sales have to pick up across the country, not just in specific states.

“In Singapore you can have one store, and it kind of covers the whole country,” explained Ang. In the US, meanwhile, “we want to make sure we can scale it across the whole nation”.

That is where Best Buy comes in. Secretlab is starting with 15 stores, and executives at both companies want “many, many more” if the tie-up works for both sides, said Ang.

However, working with Best Buy will pose a new set of challenges for the company, as it is the first time Secretlab has directly worked with a retailer. Secretlab has mostly sold online, directly to customers.

This collaboration with Best Buy means that the company will need to adopt “quite a different skill set” when it comes to managing this relationship with Best Buy, said Ang.

Still, it is not taking the collaboration lightly.

Ang noted that the retailer will serve as a sales channel, while the new experience store at West Hollywood in Los Angeles will focus on giving customers the experience.

The company chose Los Angeles as the location for its first experience centre as it is among the US cities where it has the best sales; it also has high density and the team is familiar with the location.

“You got to work with what you have… it cannot be too idealistic,” added Ang.

Not a small challenge

“The US market is very tough, especially today,” he said. Cracking it will be even more difficult than what it was 10 years ago.

States run differently, with “different rules, different values”, so you can’t run it “the way you run Singapore, where it’s just one city”, he noted.

Moreover, sales in the US are spread thin, meaning that no single city carries the market. “The US is truly very spread out, at least for us,” Ang added.

Asked about his biggest concern for the market, he replied that it used to be the “chaos in the US”, but he is less worried now, as the equipment manufacturer has diversified its supply chain to address the tariff issues.

As Secretlab seeks to expand its footprint in North America, Ang is not ruling out expansions in other parts of the world. About two months ago, the company launched sales in China through local partners, with “a few more markets” to follow.

Still, retail is not where Ang spends most of his time. He believes that the R&D of Secretlab products is what sets it apart from competitors. “We exist not because of retail or whatever. It’s because of the product.”

data.title: Q&M Dental completes Thailand acquisition with 51% stake in Bangkok clinic chain Deezy
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Q & M Dental Group (Singapore) has completed its 994.5 million baht (US$29.3 million) purchase of a 51 per cent stake in Bangkok’s Deezy dental chain, and the founders guarantee they would make a profit of about 1.25 billion baht over six years.

The company said in a bourse filing on Friday (Nov 13) that the deal gives Q&M ownership of Deezy Q & M Dental Group (Thailand), which runs the Deezy Dental Home network of 33 clinics in Bangkok and north-eastern Thailand.

The acquisition extends Q&M’s footprint beyond Singapore, Malaysia and China.

Deezy Dental Home was founded in 2017 by dentists Nanthisak Piyanantisak and Thunyaporn Pongkajornkitjakarn, who are also the guarantors of the profit target.

The company has more than 400 dentists and has served over 400,000 patients; services delivered range from general dentistry and orthodontics to cosmetic dentistry and installation of tooth implants.

The consideration comprises 700 million baht in cash and 294.5 million baht in new Q&M shares.

The cash came from a combination of bank borrowings and internal resources.

Q&M issued 16,375,714 shares to the vendor at S$0.70 apiece. They are expected to be listed on the Singapore Exchange on Monday. Trading starts at 9 am, and these shares are subject to a 15-year moratorium.

Profit guarantee

The vendor has guaranteed about 1.25 billion baht in Deezy’s audited net profit after tax for the six years from Nov 1, 2026 to Oct 31, 2032.

If there is a shortfall, it will be offset by the vendor waiving its dividend entitlements in Q&M’s favour.

Any remaining amount is to be met by Nanthisak and Thunyaporn, jointly and severally. They will draw 70.4 per cent from an escrow account and 29.6 per cent through the sale of the consideration shares, which are to be pledged to Q&M as security.

Any balance is payable in cash within 90 days of the relevant audited financial statements being determined.

If a shortfall remains unsettled after that period, Q&M may require the vendor and the guarantors to buy back the shares at the full consideration, plus simple interest of 10 per cent a year from completion.

Both founders will stay on under 15-year service agreements that include non-compete and non-solicitation terms. Thunyaporn will remain a key dentist, and Nanthisak will be in a management role.

Q&M said Deezy gives it an immediate foothold in Thailand’s private dental market without having to build operations from the ground up.

It added that the platform can be expanded through organic growth and future acquisitions, supported by rising consumer awareness, higher personal healthcare spending and growing demand for standardised dental treatments.

The group will now focus on integrating Deezy while preserving its local strengths and clinical practices. It will also share clinical and operational best practices, procurement scale and training frameworks across its regional operations.

Q&M group CEO Ng Chin Siau said: “We intend to preserve what has made Deezy successful in its home market, while bringing the group’s experience in clinical governance, procurement and dentist training to support its growth in the years ahead.”

Nanthisak said the combination would strengthen collaboration and professional development between dentists in Thailand and Singapore.

“For us, expansion is not just about (having) more clinics. It’s about better care for more patients in Thailand and South-east Asia,” he said.

Q&M, which has been listed on the mainboard of Singapore Exchange Securities Trading since 2009, has a network of more than 100 dental outlets and more than 270 dentists in Singapore .

Shares of Q&M Dental closed 1 per cent or S$0.005 lower at S$0.475 on Friday before the announcement.

data.title: Stocks to watch: SIA, CDL, Sats, AEM, StarHub, NTT DC Reit, SBS Transit, Centurion
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 12):

Singapore Airlines (SIA) : The national carrier posted net profit of S$209.7 million for its second quarter ended Sep 30, up from S$52.4 million in the previous corresponding period. This was due to stronger operating profit and a lower share of losses from associate Air India. Revenue rose 14.3 per cent to a record S$5.6 billion, while operating profit rose 16.3 per cent to S$463.7 million from a year earlier. For the first half of FY2026, SIA’s net profit fell 43.9 per cent to S$133.9 million year on year. The board declared an interim ordinary dividend of S$0.02 a share and an interim special dividend of S$0.05 a share, bringing the total payout to S$0.07 a share. Shares of SIA closed 0.4 per cent or S$0.03 higher at S$7.17 on Wednesday, before the news.

City Developments Limited (CDL) : The property group said it expects to post a “significantly weaker” financial performance for its second half ending Dec 31. Certain capital-recycling deals that the group had earlier expected to materialise in the rest of FY2026 are now expected to be completed in FY2027, it said in a business update on Wednesday. The group is also currently undertaking valuations of its property portfolio, which it noted “may give rise to impairment losses”. Shares of CDL closed 1.2 per cent or S$0.09 lower at S$7.12 on Wednesday, before the update.

Sats : The air cargo handler and airline caterer posted a 2.8 per cent rise in net profit to S$81.1 million for its second quarter ended Sep 30, from S$78.9 million in the previous corresponding period. This was due to higher cargo and meal volumes and lower tax expenses, even as the Middle East conflict raised input costs and disrupted operations, it said on Wednesday. Earnings per share stood at S$0.054 for the quarter, up from S$0.053 the year before. Revenue for the quarter rose 9 per cent to S$1.71 billion, from S$1.57 billion. Shares of Sats closed 2.6 per cent or S$0.10 higher at S$4 on Wednesday, before the news.

AEM : The semiconductor equipment maker’s net profit surged more than 18-fold to S$73.4 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from S$4 million a year earlier. Revenue rose 57.2 per cent to S$452.1 million on stronger demand for semiconductor testing solutions. AEM raised its FY2026 revenue guidance to S$680 million to S$705 million, from S$630 million to S$680 million, and its earnings per share guidance to S$0.30 to S$0.33, from S$0.245 to S$0.275. Shares of AEM closed 3.1 per cent or S$0.21 higher at S$7.05 on Wednesday.

StarHub : The telco reported a 26.3 per cent dip in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) to S$72.1 million for the third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$97.8 million the prior year. Revenue rose to S$486.8 million, up 4.5 per cent from S$464.8 million previously. The telco said that despite rising revenue, Ebitda continued to decline because of lower gross profit, higher operating expenditure and lower income from other avenues. Shares of StarHub ended flat at S$1.04 on Wednesday.

NTT DC Real Estate Investment Trust (Reit) : The Reit on Wednesday posted a distribution per unit of US$0.0432 for the first half of FY2026/27, 10 per cent above its initial public offering projection, as net property income exceeded forecasts and net finance costs came in lower than expected. For the six months ended Sep 30, distributable income stood at US$45 million, against the projected US$40.9 million. Net property income was 4.9 per cent above projection at US$55.8 million, while gross revenue came in 2 per cent higher at US$119.8 million. Units of NTT DC Reit fell 2.2 per cent or US$0.02 to close at US$0.90 on Wednesday, before the news.

SBS Transit : The public transport operator posted a 35.5 per cent rise in net profit to S$19.6 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$14.5 million in the previous corresponding period. This was due to a S$13 million write-back of prior years’ Fuel Equalisation Fund provisions, which was included in the operating profit. Operating profit for the quarter rose 37.7 per cent to S$22.6 million, from S$16.4 million in the year-ago period. Revenue fell 1.1 per cent to S$382.1 million from a year earlier due to a lower bus service fee from the loss of the Tampines package, as well as lower rail grants and ridership. Shares of SBS Transit closed flat at S$3.56 on Wednesday.

Centurion : The accommodation provider reported a 35 per cent rise in revenue to S$280.1 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from S$208.3 million in the previous corresponding period. This was mainly due to the consolidation of Westlite Mandai and new operational beds in Singapore, as well as its Harum Megah portfolio in Malaysia and Epiisod Macquarie Park in Australia. Revenue for the third quarter ended Sep 30 rose 41 per cent to S$95.2 million, it said in a business update. Shares of Centurion fell 2.4 per cent or S$0.03 to close at S$1.21 on Wednesday.

data.title: Frasers Property H2 net profit more than doubles to S$211.7 million
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Frasers Property on Friday (Nov 13) posted a 109.8 per cent increase in net profit to S$211.7 million for its second half ended Sep 30, from S$100.9 million a year earlier.

This came on the back of a 17.4 per cent increase in revenue to S$2.1 billion. Earnings per share (EPS) rose to S$0.054, from S$0.024 in the corresponding period.

For the full financial year ended Sep 30, net profit rose 23.5 per cent to S$300.1 million, from S$243.1 million a year earlier. Revenue grew 6.8 per cent to S$3.6 billion; earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) increased 10.3 per cent to S$1.4 billion.

The group said its stronger operating performance was supported by higher contributions from its Singapore retail portfolio, residential projects and industrial estates, as well as land sales.

Its full-year earnings were also lifted by net fair-value gains of S$142.3 million, versus the S$37.2 million recorded in FY2025. This mainly reflected a “valuation uplift” arising from redevelopment plans for the Valley Point site in Singapore, as well as gains from the divestment of newly completed retail assets in Australia.

Earnings per share rose to S$0.074 for FY2026, from S$0.059 a year earlier. The board has proposed a dividend of S$0.05 a share in FY2026, up from S$0.045 in FY2025.

Group CEO Panote Sirivadhanabhakdi said FY2026 was “a year of disciplined execution”.

During the year, the group released about S$4.1 billion of capital, he said, redeploying it into opportunities that “aligned with our return objectives and strengthening our balance sheet”.

“Supported by our integrated investor-developer-operator business model, we remain focused on creating resilient, long-term value for shareholders through market cycles,” he added. 

Capital recycling

Frasers Property’s capital-recycling efforts included the sale of about S$1.1 billion worth of stabilised hospitality assets under Frasers Hospitality Trust (FHT) to third-party investors.

The group said it would continue to manage the properties and earn income from the management arrangements, while moving towards a more asset-light hospitality business.

It also transferred stabilised industrial and logistics properties worth about S$500 million to its real estate investment trusts (Reits), Frasers Logistics & Commercial Trust and Frasers Property Thailand Industrial Freehold & Leasehold Reit.

Other divestments, including Australian retail assets and UK business parks, had a total value of about S$1.6 billion.

The group also brought in capital partners for its Australian industrial and logistics and hospitality assets, as well as the Valley Point redevelopment. These partnerships involved assets with a total value of about S$930 million.

Development pipeline

Frasers Property replenished its land bank during the year, expanding its residential development pipeline in “key growth corridors” in Australia and adding residential sites in Singapore and projects in China.

In Singapore, it secured two waterfront residential sites at Bayshore Drive and Kallang Close. The group also added two premium residential projects in Shanghai through joint ventures.

“Residential development continues to be a driver of cash flow and higher returns,” the group said, pointing to about S$1.1 billion of unrecognised revenue as at Sep 30.

Frasers Property is also advancing two redevelopment projects in Singapore.

At Valley Point, Frasers Property and Mitsubishi Estate Group are jointly redeveloping the Valley Point and Fraser Suites Singapore waterfront site into a mixed-use development.

The property will comprise about 407 residential units and sky villas, a 184-unit serviced residence, as well as dining, retail and lifestyle offerings. The 999-year leasehold project is targeted for launch in 2027.

Elsewhere, Yishun 10 is slated for redevelopment into a mixed-use development comprising about 110 residential units and a retail podium.

In industrial and logistics, the group delivered about 368,000 square metres of gross floor area across its markets during FY2026. Its active multi-market development pipeline stood at about 874,000 sq m.

Recurring income accounted for about 82 per cent of Frasers Property’s profit before interest, fair-value changes, tax and exceptional items in FY2026, supported by its investment property portfolio, which recorded healthy occupancy rates and positive rental reversions.

The group completed an asset enhancement initiative at Hougang Mall and commenced enhancement works at NEX during the year, as it looks to improve returns and strengthen its retail offerings.

The group is reorganising its hospitality business into two specialised platforms: Frasers Hospitality, as a dedicated lodging operations platform, and a hospitality investment and asset management business housed under group investment.

Meanwhile, Frasers Property’s net debt-to-total equity improved to 77.3 per cent as at Sep 30, from 89.2 per cent a year earlier, while net debt-to-property-assets fell to 39.9 per cent, from 43.7 per cent.

Cash and deposits increased to about S$3 billion, from S$2.4 billion. Some 73.2 per cent of borrowings were fixed-rate or hedged, with a blended cost of debt of 3.9 per cent per annum, compared with 4 per cent in FY2025.

Looking ahead, Frasers Property said it will focus on delivering its residential and industrial, and logistics development pipelines, while continuing to pursue asset management and capital-light initiatives to grow recurring and fee income.

Shares of Frasers Property closed 0.5 per cent or S$0.005 lower at S$0.91 on Friday, before the results were announced.

data.title: Issue 220: COP31âs electric dreams; Singapore tweaks green finance rules for data centres
data.description:
COP31

Aiming for a pragmatic electrification goal

Pragmatic or ineffective?

Negotiators are huddling in Turkey for this year’s United Nations climate conference under an atmosphere of muted expectations, as governments are too busy dealing with global turmoil to prioritise global warming.

The challenge is to find a common path towards credible long-term outcomes while addressing short-term needs so that climate progress is calibrated but not abandoned. This should mean continued commitment towards net-zero emissions while allowing flexibility on how to get there, prioritising renewable energy and grid improvements, and unlocking investments in climate adaptation and resilience.

Singapore Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu says that reaching a global agreement at the conference known as COP31 will be more difficult than in previous years.

“The headwind is getting stronger, not weaker,” she says.

Indeed, the war in Iran and the massive data centre build-out driven by artificial intelligence has placed energy security at the top of mind for most governments. While this has helped to spur interest in renewables, it has also extinguished plans to phase out coal in countries like Indonesia that have domestic sources of the high-carbon fuel.

The economic uncertainties brought about by a fractured global trade system and the energy-led inflationary shock have also dampened growth expectations and lowered fiscal headroom for climate-related spending and investment.

Under such circumstances, the joint presidents of COP31 – Turkey and Australia – are pushing for a “35-by-35” goal to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity to at least 35 per cent by 2035, from about 20 per cent at the moment.

It’s a target seemingly picked because it seems easy to accept in the face of all these headwinds. After all, the International Energy Agency estimates that current policies are already on a trajectory to reach 29 per cent electrification by 2035, so while going for 35 per cent might take more effort, it is still somewhat feasible. The increasingly competitive pricing of electric vehicles and battery solutions, as well as the data centre boom, suggest that the world is already headed in the right direction.

The COP31 presidents are also suggesting that the target give parties the flexibility to decide the energy supply mix, which will allow countries at different stages of development and with different levels of resources to choose energy transition pathways most appropriate to their circumstances.

Therein lies the rub. Setting an electrification target without binding it to emissions reductions or a higher share of renewable generation risks creating a meaningless goal, because electrification supported by renewables generation has a substantially different impact on emissions reduction from electrification supported by fossil fuel generation. It’s like ordering a cake without specifying the occasion it’s meant to celebrate or the type of cake desired. You’ll get your cake, but it might not be the one you were hoping to eat.

The rigour of the 35-by-35 target is likely to be a source of much debate, but a pragmatic goal that nudges all countries in the right direction is better than no agreement. Nevertheless, there can be a fine line between a pragmatic consensus and a meaningless one. Negotiators will have to work for the former.

The first step is to connect electrification with emissions goals, because mitigating greenhouse gas emissions is ultimately the objective of the climate conference. Without that north star, an electrification target could end up going nowhere.

Low-carbon generation must be an integral part of electrification, although the pace at which the transition occurs could afford some flexibility to countries that need it. Many developing countries will fall into that category. However, COP31 needs to deliver better support for emerging and developing countries to build low-carbon electricity generation and to modernise and improve their grid infrastructure to handle the increased electricity demand and to firm their network to handle the intermittency of renewable energy.

The high curtailment rate of renewable energy in certain parts of China demonstrates the importance of upgrading electrical grids when renewable generation scales up. Grid modernisation is an important enabling investment even in electrification strategies that are still heavily reliant on coal or natural gas generation. That is because the grid will be able to handle more renewable power in the future.

Beyond electrification, COP31 needs to take steps towards raising investments in climate adaptation and resilience. The current expectation is that global warming will overshoot the 1.5 deg C threshold. Emerging and developed countries – such as those in South-east Asia – are especially vulnerable to disruptions from climate change. The adaptation investment gap remains significant and needs to be closed.

Being pragmatic should not mean becoming less ambitious. Rather, it should be about realigning ambitions towards more viable areas. Electrification is a fine goal in the current environment, but it should be aimed strategically.

Sustainable finance

Looking past data centres’ efficiency

Singapore’s sustainable finance eligibility criteria for data centres may have a blind spot when it comes to assessing a centre’s impact on surrounding communities and ecosystems.

An update to the Singapore-Asia Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance – which sets the conditions under which various economic activities can qualify for sustainable financing – includes revisions to criteria for data centres that better recognise trade-offs between power and water efficiency.

Data centres are either air-cooled or water-cooled. An air-cooled data centre can be very water-efficient but will be less efficient in its electricity usage; conversely, a water-cooled data centre consumes more water but is more efficient in its power usage.

A data centre development outside Singapore pursuing green financing under the earlier version of the Taxonomy had to meet the platinum rating under Singapore’s Green Mark Scheme for data centres with regard to power efficiency, as well as a single water efficiency hurdle.

The revised green financing criteria relaxes power efficiency requirements for data centres built with tighter water constraints, encouraging optimisation of resources instead of improving one aspect at the expense of the other.

But while the taxonomy ensures that data centres obtaining sustainable financing under its criteria are broadly efficient, it does not have a robust approach to address the external impact of data centres on their surroundings.

Consider recent negative news coverage of official investigations into Google’s felling of forests in Finland for its data centre, as well as NextDC’s delays to projects amid community protests in Australia. The fact is that a large data centre has a substantial impact on its surrounding environment and communities by virtue of the scale of its physical footprint, of its emissions and of its absolute consumption of resources, regardless of the data centre’s efficiency.

Some additional criteria worth considering could be requirements for environmental impact assessments or community engagement to be carried out and adjudicated, or compliance with local policies that adequately cover those impacts.

External impact presents a risk if not properly addressed. Investors holding what they think is a sustainable bond may find the funded project generating negative impact, which could affect the value of the asset.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Singtel, ST Engg, Genting, First Resources, Golden Agri, CDG, Bumitama, Food Empire
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 13):

Singtel : The telecommunications giant on Friday posted a 55 per cent decline in net profit to S$1.54 billion for the first half-year ended September, from S$3.4 billion in the year-ago period. This was mainly due to the absence of S$2.21 billion in net exceptional gains recorded a year earlier from the partial sale of its stake in Airtel and the Intouch-Gulf Energy merger. Excluding exceptional items, underlying net profit rose 10 per cent to S$1.49 billion, from S$1.35 billion a year earlier. The company declared a 10 per cent higher interim dividend of S$0.09 per share. Singtel closed S$0.01 or 0.2 per cent higher at S$4.15 on Thursday.

ST Engineering : The technology and engineering group posted a 9 per cent year-on-year increase in revenue to S$3.4 billion for the third quarter ended September, from S$3.1 billion a year earlier, it said on Friday. It also declared a third-quarter interim dividend of S$0.05 per share, up from S$0.04 a year earlier. Together with its first- and second-quarter dividends of S$0.04 and S$0.05 per share, respectively, this brings the total dividend for the first nine months to S$0.14 per share. ST Engineering closed S$0.02 or 0.2 per cent higher at S$9.76 on Thursday.

Genting Singapore : The integrated resort operator posted a 42.2 per cent fall in net profit to S$54.7 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$94.6 million in the corresponding year-ago period. Revenue for the quarter fell 12.9 per cent to S$566.1 million, from S$649.8 million a year earlier. Gaming revenue at Resorts World Sentosa (RWS), the group’s Singapore integrated resort, dropped 21.7 per cent to S$315 million in Q3, from S$402.3 million in the year-ago period. Genting Singapore said that renewal works at RWS will constrain operating capacity through 2027. Genting Singapore closed Thursday at S$0.61, down S$0.005 or 0.8 per cent.

First Resources : The palm oil producer posted a 40.1 per cent rise in its underlying net profit to US$122.7 million for the third quarter ended Sep 30, from US$87.5 million a year ago. The increase was boosted by higher sales of palm oil products and fruit bunches harvested from oil palm plants, it said. Sales was up 24.9 per cent to US$578.6 million for the quarter, compared with US$463.3 million a year ago. The group said it expects demand for palm oil to remain supported by Indonesia’s biodiesel programme. Shares of First Resources closed flat at S$2.79 on Thursday.

Golden Agri-Resources : The palm oil company posted a net profit of US$162 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30, a 32 per cent increase from US$123 million in the previous quarter. The rise in net profit was due primarily to higher plantation output and investment income received in Q3 2026, the company said. Revenue for Q3 was up 3 per cent at US$3.5 billion on a quarterly basis, supported by an appreciation in crude palm oil prices. Its shares ended Thursday 1.9 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.27.

ComfortDelGro (CDG) : The taxi operator posted a 20 per cent fall in net profit to S$141.1 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from S$176.4 million in the previous corresponding period. It said its taxi and private-hire business was hit by competition and cautious consumer spending. Revenue for the nine months rose 4.9 per cent to S$3.94 billion from S$3.75 billion the year before, supported by contracted public transport operations. The company is bidding for more public transport contracts, with opportunities available from 2026 to 2028 estimated at more than S$17 billion. CDG closed flat at S$1.29 on Thursday.

Bumitama : The palm oil producer reported a 2 per cent increase in its net profit to 614 billion rupiah (US$34 million) for the quarter ended Sep 30, 2026, compared with 603 billion rupiah from the corresponding period a year ago. For the nine months ended Sep 30, 2026, net profit rose 31 per cent to 2.4 trillion rupiah from a year ago. The company said its performance was supported by improvements in productivity in its plantations and mills, particularly during the earlier part of the quarter. Shares of Bumitama closed flat at S$1.39 on Thursday.

Food Empire : The company posted an 11.7 per cent rise in revenue to a record US$476.5 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from US$426.7 million in the previous corresponding period. This was driven mainly by its core Russia and Central Asia segments. For its third quarter ended Sep 30, revenue rose 5.8 per cent to US$161.4 million, from US$152.6 million a year earlier. This was driven by growth across its core segments and partly offset by a 5.2 per cent decline in Europe. Food Empire closed flat at S$1.79 on Thursday.

data.title: European stocks near record highs, US dollar gains on Fed rate hike bets
data.description:
[PARIS] European stocks held near record highs on Friday (Nov 13), after a week dominated by Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Meanwhile, the greenback was close to a 19-month high on the possibility of a bigger-than-expected rate hike by the US Federal Reserve in December.

Huang resigned as CEO of the American chipmaker on Thursday.

His departure could have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy and the broader artificial intelligence industry and supply chain, given Huang’s push to preserve access to the Chinese market and his close ties with US President Donald Trump.

The US Justice Department said it does not know whether the Chinese businesswoman at the centre of the scandal was a spy.

AI-related shares in China dropped after Huang’s resignation, but indices in Taiwan, Japan and South Korea gained overnight as traders shrugged off concerns about the scandal’s impact on the global AI boom.

“Jensen Huang clearly has been a very high profile CEO and he is associated with the massive success that Nvidia has had. What we can’t be sure of is the role of that one key individual to the plans at Nvidia,” said Tristan Hanson, multi-asset fund manager at M&G.

“It’s important news and we’re going to have to watch to see how the situation develops, but the AI theme is much bigger than Jensen Huang ...The AI technology boom is not about one individual.”

Europe’s Stoxx 600, which hit a record high in the previous session, was up by less than 0.1 per cent on the day at 1015 GMT and on track for a weekly gain.

London’s FTSE 100 was up 0.2 per cent while Germany’s DAX was up by less than 0.1 per cent .

The MSCI World Equity Index was down by less than 0.1 per cent.

Microsoft said its Outlook, Teams and Copilot were down, causing disruptions at trading firms and delays to companies publishing their results.

US dollar up, traders bet on rate hikes

The US dollar index was at 103.19, having earlier hit its highest since April 2025, as traders increased their bets that the Fed could do a larger-than-expected 50 basis point rate hike in December.

US inflation data on Tuesday showed a third consecutive month of food and accommodation getting more expensive, and remarks by some Fed officials were seen as hawkish.

Investors now see a 12 per cent chance of a jumbo 50 basis point Fed hike in December, up from zero a week ago, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

US Treasury yields rose, with the two-year yield hitting a one-month high.

European government bond yields were up, with the German 10-year yield at 3.3668 per cent. The euro was flat at US$1.1054.

M&G’s Hanson said that more rate hikes “might look a bit hasty”, as he expects some of the factors causing inflation – including the oil shock – to lessen in future.

Oil prices were headed for a second weekly decline, after a volatile week in which earlier hopes for a rapprochement in the US-Israeli war on Iran were offset by strikes on Saudi Arabian infrastructure by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and attacks on tankers shipping crude out of the Gulf.

Brent crude futures were down 0.4 per cent at US$95.45 a barrel while US crude eased 0.8 per cent to US$88.04 per barrel.

Spot gold gained 0.5 per cent to US$3,897.36 an ounce. REUTERS

data.title: Microsoft outage sends traders back to phones and fax
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Traders were forced to do business by phone and Whatsapp, and even fire up their fax machines, as a worldwide outage of Microsoft software crippled communications and snarled e-mail services at stock exchanges. 

In Singapore, traders reported some banks’ inability to complete financing deals, while Euronext, Nasdaq and Deutsche Boerse said they were having e-mail issues.

Japanese firms said trades were happening by fax and Indian brokerages said there could be a delay in responding to e-mailed queries.

The outage left Kenneth Goh, who is travelling for work in Malaysia, unable to get market updates that help inform his advice to private clients.

“It has been super irritating,” said Goh, director of private wealth management at broker UOB Kay Hian, who was relying on patchy phone calls to speak with clients. “If the outage crosses 24 hours, then we’d be in the red zone.”

Goh’s experience was echoed by many after Microsoft suffered one of its most severe disruptions in recent memory.

It is still struggling to restore access to some of its flagship software half a day after an outage began, affecting its Outlook, Teams and Copilot systems.

The issues hindered workflows on trading desks, delayed corporate disclosure and even caused Cartier owner Richemont to briefly delay the release of its earnings statement.

Microsoft said in a status update on Friday (Nov 13) that it was seeing “positive signs for server stability”, though services have not been restored.

Trading in global markets was relatively calm, with S&P 500 futures little changed. 

Ryutaro Kimura, a Tokyo-based senior bond strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management, said while trading itself is largely unaffected, “confirmations backed up, creating settlement headaches for back offices”.

“Desks were still getting trades done by phone and fax,” he added.

Meanwhile, CMC Markets traders resorted to “old-school” trading as Microsoft’s systems went offline. 

“Everyone was back on the phone, and our WhatsApp chats were busier than usual,” said Eugene Koh, sales trader at CMC Markets Singapore.

“Something that normally takes a second on e-mail might now take a phone call and a few minutes to get through.”

Andy Kent, a London-based broker at Kyte Broking, said the outage was affecting the processing of trades more than the ability to make them.

“This will have an impact on liquidity as institutions will be less keen to trade until the straight-through processing functions are back up and running,” said Kent.

Matthew Haupt, a portfolio manager at Wilson Asset Management, said the firm’s small cap team told him that some trading volumes in equities have fallen on the back of the blackout. 

After a turbulent run in markets with the ousting of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and hot inflation print, traders said the communications failure was another major headache to end the week. 

“Outlook is the appendix of the modern financial operations world,” said Calvin Yeoh, a portfolio manager at Blue Edge Advisors.

“So aside from the entire front to back infrastructure of global finance being crippled, and with Nvidia melting down and rates markets going wild this week, yeah it’s been all good.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Indonesiaâs upper house to pick new vice-president on Dec 2, its speaker says
data.description:
[JAKARTA] Indonesia’s upper house of parliament will pick the country’s new vice-president on Dec 2, its speaker said on Friday (Nov 13), after the dramatic resignation of Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the president’s deputy and the son of his predecessor.

Gibran’s resignation this week, which analysts say could widen the gulf between President Prabowo Subianto and former President Joko Widodo, followed a month of increasing political pressure from lawmakers after Indonesia’s top courts ruled that he had inadequate education credentials to run for the job.

Speaker Ahmad Muzani said the upper house, which is tasked by law with appointing the new vice-president, would now send a letter to Prabowo requesting that he submit two names for the job.

The house has also formed a team of 36 lawmakers to verify the candidates’ credentials, Muzani said. It was not immediately clear which names Prabowo would submit.

On Thursday, Gibran said his resignation was a personal decision and unrelated to issues pertaining to his education credentials.

Political turbulence

Gibran, 39, was elected alongside Prabowo in the 2024 election.

Critics accused his father, Widodo, better known as Jokowi, of meddling in the process by influencing a court decision that changed the election rules, enabling Gibran to stand.

Analysts believe Gibran’s resignation could stoke further political turbulence and lock Jokowi and Prabowo into a bitter rivalry.

Jokowi defeated Prabowo in two presidential elections, in 2014 and 2019. During Jokowi’s second term, he made Prabowo his defence minister and tacitly supported the latter’s 2024 presidential run.

On Thursday, however, both Jokowi and Gibran struck a conciliatory tone and said they would continue to support Prabowo.

Gibran, in a video address to volunteers shown by news channel Kompas TV, said he would not be in opposition even as an outsider to Prabowo’s administration.

“I only have one message: Please, inside or outside government, we still have to support the president,” he said.

Analysts said another sign of the gulf between Prabowo and Jokowi was last week’s police revelation of an inquiry into suspected illegal wiretapping by four senior police officials, including former police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who is widely seen as a Jokowi loyalist.

Police said on Thursday they had enough initial evidence to pursue treason charges against the four suspects for wiretapping Prabowo, other politicians, activists and journalists.

Reuters has been unable to reach the suspects for comment. REUTERS
